You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.

Which model showed debt underutilization in this study?

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

1	Since Modigliani and Miller (1958), economists have relaxed many of their
     2	assumptions to understand the observed behavior of leverage ratios. Arguably,
     3	the trade-off theory has emerged as one of the leading paradigms, even though
     4	it has been often challenged by empirical tests that appear to favor other
     5	theories or suggest taxes are not that important. Therefore, there is still no
     6	consensus in the literature. Moreover, none of the extant theories jointly
     7	address the following questions in a parsimonious and simple framework:
     8	(1) why firms tend to use debt financing so conservatively, (2) whether there
     9	is indeed a target leverage ratio and partial adjustment toward it, (3) why the leverage-growth
    10	relation is negative, and (4) why average leverage paths
    11	persist for over two decades.
    12	To answers these questions, we extend Hackbarth and Mauer (2012) to
    13	multiple financing and investment decisions that maximize initial value. We
    14	develop two versions of a dynamic model with endogenous financing and
    15	investment decisions. While the multistage model features two sequentially
    16	exercisable investment options, the single-stage model has only one investment option. The
    17	single-stage model serves as a benchmark to gauge
    18	investment-financing interactions in the multistage model. In both versions,
    19	the capital expenditure is funded by a mix of debt and equity. This mixture not
    20	only trades off tax benefits of debt against bankruptcy costs (triggered by an
    21	endogenous default decision) but also recognizes financial flexibility in the
    22	multistage model.
    23	The solution of the dynamic model offers a rich set of novel predictions that
    24	link the behavior of a firm’s leverage ratios to its investment opportunities.
    25	First, a role for financial flexibility emerges endogenously because dynamic
    26	financing-investment interactions between stages lead to an “intertemporal
    27	effect” in the multistage model: reaping investment (i.e., cash flow) and tax
    28	benefits sooner by issuing more debt in the first stage to fund the investment
    29	cost reduces financial flexibility for funding more of the investment cost with
    30	debt in the second stage. In comparison to the single-stage model, firms
    31	underutilize debt in the multistage model when financing investment the first
    32	time to retain financial flexibility. Because both debt issues jointly optimize
    33	initial equity value (and hence internalize dilutive externalities on each other),
    34	underutilization of debt persists when firms mature (i.e., exercise their last
    35	investment options), and underutilization is more (less) severe for more backloaded (front-loaded)
    36	investment opportunities. It is worth noting that leverage
    37	does not vary with investment in the single-stage model. Only in the multistage model leverage
    38	dynamics crucially hinge on the structure of the investment process in that it creates significant
    39	variation target leverage ratios.1
    40	Second, optimizing behavior by firms in a dynamic trade-off model with
    41	investment generates a significant fraction of low or zero leverage firms and
    42	path-dependent, persistent leverage ratios. Our analysis shows how incentives
    43	to retain financial flexibility in the first stage crucially depend on the structure
    44	of the investment process. Given the wide range of optimal target leverage
    45	ratios, the model suggests that leverage ratios can greatly vary depending on
    46	how the firm grows assets-in-place by exercising its real options.
    47	Third, structural models without dynamic financing-investment interactions
    48	(1) overestimate target leverage ratios, and (2) can be misleading in that they
    49	imply a fixed target leverage ratio that is largely taken to be exogenous to the
    50	investment process. It thus seems difficult to determine target leverage in the conventional sense.
    51	This also suggests that there is no meaningful measurement of partial adjustment toward target
    52	leverage (as in, e.g., Flannery and
    53	Rangan 2006) without recognizing the structure of the investment process.2
    54	To test the model’s ability to match observed outcomes, we estimate key
    55	model parameters via simulated method of moments (SMM). Intuitively,
    56	SMM finds the set of parameters, which minimizes the difference of the
    57	simulated model moments and the data moments from COMPUSTAT’s
    58	annual tapes for the period of 1965 to 2009. We then split the full sample
    59	into low, medium, and high market-to-book (or q) subsamples and employ
    60	SMM also to fit the four parameters for each subsample. We split the sample
    61	based on q to proxy for investment opportunities. Low q firms tend to have
    62	fewer investment opportunities, whereas high q firms tend to have more
    63	investment opportunities. Therefore, the relative value of q is informative
    64	about the structure of the investment process in the real data. Our estimation
    65	results reveal that high q firms have the most back-loaded investment processes, and low q firms
    66	have the most front-loaded ones.
    67	Graham (2000) reports that firms, even stable and profitable, use less debt
    68	than predicted by the static view of the tax benefits of debt. Two of five firms
    69	have an average leverage ratio of less than 20%, and the median firm uses
    70	only 31.4% leverage over the 1965 to 2000 period, which implies a “low
    71	leverage puzzle.” More recently, Strebulaev and Yang (2013) find that on
    72	average 10% of firms have zero leverage and almost 22% firms have less
    73	than 5% quasi-market leverage, which represents a “zero leverage puzzle.”
    74	We emphasize the importance of real frictions in a dynamic trade-off model
    75	and thereby provide an economically meaningful mechanism for why firms
    76	tend to use debt financing so conservatively. Based on the structural estimation results for the
    77	full sample, the simulated economies feature a significant
    78	fraction of low (and zero) leverage firms. Moreover, in contrast to much
    79	higher point estimates in prior studies, we report, on average, 20% leverage
    80	in dynamics (i.e., for all firms) and 19% at investment points (i.e., for investing firms).
    81	In addition, we perform capital structure regressions on simulated data and
    82	show that the model can replicate stylized facts established by empirical
    83	research. In the spirit of Strebulaev (2007), simulation of the multistage model
    84	of corporate investment and financing dynamics reinforces the need to differentiate investment
    85	points from other data points when interpreting coefficient
    86	estimates for market-to-book or profitability in a dynamic world. Consistent
    87	with Frank and Goyal (2009) and others, we find leverage is negatively related
    88	to the risk of cash flows, the cost of bankruptcy, and market-to-book, but
    89	positively related the size of the firm and the tax rate. Finally, we document that real frictions
    90	in a dynamic model can produce
    91	average leverage paths that closely resemble the ones in the data (e.g.,
    92	Lemmon, Roberts, and Zender 2008).3 That is, endogenous investment and
    93	financing decisions in a dynamic model can largely explain the otherwise
    94	puzzling patterns that, despite of some convergence, average leverage ratios
    95	across portfolios are fairly stable over time for both types of sorts (i.e., actual
    96	and unexpected leverage) performed by these authors.4 To do so, we extend
    97	the multistage model to randomly imposed initial variation in leverage. If
    98	model firms are “born” with high (low) leverage ratios at the beginning,
